failure_modes.description: Local controllers cannot accurately measure traffic flow in real-world conditions with sensor errors, weather effects, and vehicle detection failures
failure_modes.evidence: Traffic sensor failure rates are estimated at 10-15% in urban environments, leading to incorrect flow measurements that would corrupt the feedback mechanism

failure_modes.description: Positive feedback in traffic systems leads to Braess's paradox where adding capacity can reduce overall network performance
failure_modes.evidence: Numerous studies have shown that uncoordinated local optimization can create worse system-wide performance than fixed-time signals

failure_modes.description: The mechanism fails to account for pedestrian and bicycle traffic which requires different timing logic
failure_modes.evidence: Urban intersections must balance multiple transportation modes, and vehicle-focused optimization would create dangerous conditions for pedestrians

failure_modes.description: The system would exhibit persistent oscillations between adjacent intersections with conflicting timing
failure_modes.evidence: Existing adaptive signal systems require inter-communication to prevent exactly this failure mode, which this hypothesis explicitly rejects

failure_modes.description: Network-wide optimization cannot emerge from purely local decisions in non-convex optimization problems like traffic flow
failure_modes.evidence: Traffic flow optimization is a known non-convex problem where local optima do not guarantee global optimality

failure_modes.description: Similar decentralized approaches have been tried and failed in real-world implementations
failure_modes.evidence: The TRANSYT and SCOOT systems from the 1970s already demonstrated that some coordination is necessary for effective traffic optimization
